title: Bhajan

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pujari, the priest at the front. Your line was someone holds the form. Did you thank someone who keeps something going? Day one hundred and thirty-six.

It's a Saturday evening in somebody's living room. The sofas have been pushed against the wall and there are sheets on the carpet. An uncle sits at a harmonium, pumping the bellows with one hand. A teenager drums on a dholak. An auntie has tiny brass cymbals that go ching, ching, ching. Thirty people sit on the floor. Some have lyric sheets, most don't need them. Nobody is a professional. Half of them are off-key. And by the third song, the whole room is singing so loudly the neighbors can hear. Today: bhajan.
screen: `SOFAS AGAINST THE WALL.` → `HARMONIUM, DRUM, TINY CYMBALS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM, SINGING LOUD.`

segments.voice: Bhajan is a devotional song. The word comes from the Sanskrit root bhaj, which means to share in, to belong to, to adore. It's the same root as bhakti, your sixteenth word: devotion is a verb. A bhajan is bhakti you can sing. Bhajans are usually simple. Short lines, a lot of repetition, melodies anyone can pick up by the second time through. And they're in the languages people actually speak: Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Bengali, Tamil, Kannada, and many more. Many were written by the poet-saints of medieval India, singers who wanted God in the everyday language of the street. Mirabai, a sixteenth-century Rajput princess who left palace life singing for Krishna. Surdas and Tulsidas. Tukaram in Maharashtra. Their songs are still sung in living rooms every weekend. Some bhajans are very short. One that many people know, famous in part because Gandhi loved it, begins: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Lord of the line of Raghu, King Ram; purifier of the fallen, Sita and Ram. Now, why sing it in a group, and why loud? Because a group bhajan does something quiet prayer can't. Your voice disappears into everyone else's. You stop hearing whether you're good. For a few minutes, you're not a person worrying; you're part of one big sound. The tradition doesn't ask for a pretty voice. It asks for a whole one.
screen: `BHAJ: TO SHARE IN, TO ADORE.` · `SIMPLE, REPEATED, EVERYDAY WORDS.` · `THE POET-SAINTS: MIRABAI, TUKARAM.` · `NOT PRETTY. WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Let's sing, and if you're somewhere you can't, sing inside. Try the line: Raghupati raghava raja ram, patita pavana sita ram. Once, slowly. Again, a little louder than feels comfortable. Again, and don't worry about the tune. If you'd rather, sing any song of devotion or gratitude you already know, from any part of your life. Let the sound fill your chest. Then stop, and sit in the ringing quiet afterward. The bell holds the time.
Bhajan. A devotional song, simple and repeated, in everyday language, usually sung together, and usually loud. Today's word.
Your line: loud. Today, sing one song all the way through, out loud, in the shower, in the car, anywhere, without caring how it sounds. Day one hundred and thirty-six.

howItsDone: Many Hindus gather in homes and temples, often weekly, to sing bhajans, simple devotional songs in regional languages, many written by medieval poet-saints, with harmonium, drums and small cymbals.

original.note: Sanskrit/Hindi bhajana: adoration; a devotional song. From the root bhaj, as in bhakti.

trapdoor: what it means: bhakti you can sing: simple, repeated, in everyday language, sung together until you're part of one sound.

what a scholar hears: bhajana and bhakti share the root bhaj; the medieval bhakti poet-saints (Mirabai, Surdas, Tulsidas, Tukaram, and many others) composed in vernacular languages, and their songs form much of today's bhajan repertoire.

notes: Raghupati raghava raja ram: the opening line is quoted in transliteration from the traditional original; its authorship is disputed (often traced to Lakshmanacharya, popularized by Vishnu Digambar Paluskar and Gandhi). The gloss is the writer's own. Please confirm.
Mirabai as a sixteenth-century Rajput princess is standard but her biography is largely hagiographic; confirm wording.
Harmonium, dholak and manjira/kartal (small cymbals) are the common instruments; varies by region.
